name: Erik Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, political parties and government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. This conversation is confidential, and your name won't be attached. Tell me about a working day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the evening repairs queue for a housing-service contact centre. Tenants ring when a leak comes back or a contractor has not turned up, and I trace the ticket and call the crew before promising anything. I have a two-year college diploma in office administration and have become one of the better agents here, but my lead rate is still low for this work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What helps you do it, and who is at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I can remember which block has the old boilers, and I keep a paper map of the contractor routes. I have never used the AI helper; the ticket number and a phone call serve me better. My wife Ruth cleans at a clinic, our grown son has his own rent, and we have about three weeks of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say on the floor that a little faster typing doesn't mend a leaking pipe. A tenant needs the right contractor at the right flat, and the supervisor should leave us time to check the ticket.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect people will keep ringing us, so I do not see a lost job here. Ruth's clinic rota changes each month, and three weeks saved means a missed shift still hurts our rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would keep checking the ticket number against my route map and ask for the next month's paid evening rota in writing. In the first year of AI Plateau, Ruth and I would keep the old kitchen cupboards another year rather than borrow for new ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a short pay month, though the work itself looks steady. The flat does not care whether AI was exciting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake would faster typing miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A contractor once drove to number 18 when the call came from 81, and we lost the afternoon fixing it. A faster message would have sent the contractor to the wrong flat faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could your son help with a short month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son can visit for supper, but his own rent takes most of his wage. I will not put his money into our household plan.

say: I would tell colleagues **ticket checks** matter more than faster messages.
I would ask for the **paid evening rota** in writing.
think: I expect **repair calls** to continue, but my household income remains fragile.
I worry **three weeks saved** cannot cover Ruth's short clinic month.
do: Keep checking **repair tickets** against contractor routes and request the written evening rota.
Delay **new kitchen cupboards** rather than borrow while our reserve is thin.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent during a short pay month.
S0.quote: A faster message would have sent the contractor to the wrong flat faster.
fieldNote: His **senior skill** protects calls, yet low pay and variable household hours expose rent.
He avoids **new borrowing** for cupboards while the reserve is thin.

steps.text: Keep checking repair tickets against contractor routes and request the next paid evening rota
Keep the working kitchen cupboards another year rather than borrow for replacements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that software can book a routine repair but cannot smell a damp wall over the phone. I would ask management to show which evening complaint hours remain paid before cutting the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My difficult cases may stay, but one lead could cover two queues while the simple tickets vanish. That could cut my own hours, and Ruth's variable wage would not fill the gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep a week of repeat-leak tickets and ask the manager for the planned paid hours on the complex queue. If my evening hours fall in the first year routine bookings move, I would check posted local housing desks, but I would take another job only if its written weekly hours and wages cover our rent and bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a smaller paid week. A title can remain while the paid week shrinks. I am not slow to understand the risk just because I dislike the software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you count a repeat leak?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count a leak again if the tenant calls after a bot says the job is complete. The second call and the second visit are real work on the same pipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could the household cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth and I would cut the paid television package if my rota lost a day. It is a small saving, and I would still need paid work to make up the missing shift.

say: I would ask for **paid complex-case hours** before management cuts the rota.
I would say **repeat leaks** still need people and visits.
think: I could lose **evening hours** even while retaining a lead title.
I cannot replace a lost day with Ruth's **variable clinic wage**.
do: Log **repeat-leak tickets** and request the paid complex-queue rota.
Cut **paid television** if my rota loses a day; check posted desks if hours fall.
Take another job only with written **weekly wages and hours** covering rent and bus fare.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a smaller paid week.
S1.quote: A title can remain while the paid week shrinks.
fieldNote: His lead title is **not a wage guarantee** when queues combine.
He names a **small spending cut**, while a replacement job needs written weekly terms.

steps.text: Log repeat-leak tickets and request the planned paid complex-queue rota
Cut the paid television package if Erik loses an evening shift
After hours fall, check posted housing desks; take only written rent-and-bus-covering weekly wages and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2028 can handle booking and arguing over repair tickets, while hands-on repair robots follow around 2031. That leaves my desk in trouble first, even if the pipe still needs fixing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of our paid calls could end in a short stretch. Three weeks of savings and Ruth's cleaning wage cannot carry rent for months while I wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 I would ask the manager for the written date of any rota change and put our rent, food and heating on one page with Ruth. If most of my hours end in the first year after 2028, I would apply for posted paid housing or clinic reception work; I would accept only written weekly wages and hours covering our bills after bus fare, and keep any paid calls still offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed; the rent date is much nearer than a new skill. I can still ask employers for real hours instead of sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in a reception advert?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the advertised reception rota includes five mornings or just one relief day. We cannot eat a job title for breakfast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the rent payment is missed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I do not expect our son to pay rent for us. If we actually missed a payment, Ruth and I would ask the landlord for a schedule rather than hide the letter.

say: I would say **2028 thinking AI** reaches tickets before 2031 repair robots.
I would ask for a **written rota-change date** at work.
think: I expect **most paid calls** could end quickly.
I cannot cover **months of rent** from three weeks saved and Ruth's wage.
do: Request the **written rota date** and list rent, food and heating with Ruth.
If most **2028 hours end**, apply for posted reception; accept only written after-bus-fare weekly wages and hours covering bills.
Ask the landlord for a **payment schedule** only if rent is actually missed.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by a likely major paid-hours loss.
S2.quote: We cannot eat a job title for breakfast.
fieldNote: He expects a **fast hours loss** on screen work while repairs remain physical.
He would seek a **landlord schedule** only after an actual missed rent payment.

steps.text: Keep any paid repair calls and ask for the written rota-change date
If most 2028 hours end, apply for posted paid local reception work
Accept only written weekly wages and hours covering bills after bus fare
If rent is actually missed, ask landlord for a payment schedule

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the floor that five years is enough to notice if the queue is shrinking, provided we can see paid hours by month. Thinking AI reaches desk repairs in 2031; robots reach the hands-on work around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep the complex calls longer, but I cannot count on the evening rota holding until I am 63. I do not know what income Ruth and I could live on without our wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask the shift manager for quarterly paid-hour figures for the complex repair queue and keep my own log of repeat leaks. If my hours fall after 2031, I would visit the nearby clinic desk to ask about posted paid reception shifts and their actual bus times before applying; I would keep current paid calls until a written bill-covering weekly offer existed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though I have time to watch a real trend. A long warning is useful only if somebody shows us the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the quarterly comparison show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the complex-call hours beside the repeat tickets for the same quarter. If the calls stay busy but our hours fall, the figures show exactly where the saving came from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might want fewer evenings by 63, but that is not a retirement plan. Ruth and I would need actual income statements before deciding whether we can afford any reduction.

say: I would ask for **quarterly paid-hour figures** on complex repairs.
I would explain **2031 desk AI** comes before 2034 repair robots.
think: I cannot assume my **evening rota** lasts until 63 or pays the same amount.
I cannot assume **replacement income** without actual household income statements.
do: Log **repeat leaks** and request quarterly paid-hour figures in 2026.
If hours fall after 2031, visit clinic for **posted paid shifts** and bus times before applying.
Keep **current paid calls** until a written weekly offer covers our bills.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a possible hours cut, with time to track it.
S3.quote: A long warning is useful only if somebody shows us the rota.
fieldNote: His **quarterly comparison** tests whether busy calls coexist with fewer paid hours.
He checks **bus times** and written pay before leaving a current paid shift.

steps.text: Log repeat repair calls and request quarterly complex-queue paid-hour figures
If hours fall after 2031, ask nearby clinic about posted paid shifts and bus times
Keep paid calls until a written weekly offer covers household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ruth a decade gives us time to put the bills and the hours on one sheet each year. Full thinking AI comes to repair tickets by 2036, with hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might still need an income from work. Three weeks saved is not a pension. I will not say we can stop simply because our children are grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2026 we would collect actual income statements and total twelve months of rent and bills. I would keep the paid repair queue while it exists and ask for the written evening rota each year; in the first year after 2036 I would keep working if verified income cannot cover the flat, and inspect real paid shifts then available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about this month's rent as well as later life. Ten years helps with planning, but does not fill a thin reserve today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare each year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would set our actual wages beside rent and ask how many paid evenings remain, not how many complaints the system closed. A yearly comparison is work we can do without believing a pension number we have not checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your son help later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son is welcome at the table, but his wages pay his own household. Ruth and I will only count support if somebody really offers it; I do not want to build a plan from an imagined gift.

say: I would use the **decade** to compare actual wages and bills yearly.
I would say **2036 desk AI** comes before 2039 repair robots.
think: I may still **need wages at 68** with only a thin reserve now.
I cannot assume a **pension amount** or grown-child support.
do: Collect **actual income statements** and compare a year of rent and bills.
Keep **paid repair calls** and request the evening rota yearly; after 2036 continue if verified income falls short.
If verified income falls short after 2036, inspect **actually available paid shifts** before changing work.
feel: I feel **anxious** about rent now and uncertain income later.
S4.quote: Three weeks saved is not a pension.
fieldNote: His **retirement choices** depend on verified wages and bills, not age alone.
He keeps **grown-child support** conditional on an actual offer instead of assuming that help is available.

steps.text: Keep paid repair calls and request the written evening rota each year
Compare actual income statements with twelve months of rent and bills while keeping paid work
If verified income falls short after 2036, inspect actually available paid shifts

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because a call rota can vanish long before the pipes stop leaking. Written paid hours and a posted local job that covers rent after the bus would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what a lead actually takes home, not just whether he has a lead title. A title does not pay our rent.

headlineQuote: A title does not pay our rent.
portrait: A **58-year-old** repair-call lead with a two-year college diploma and strong job skill.
He **never uses AI**, relying on ticket numbers and contractor routes.
His **low lead wage** and Ruth's changing clinic shifts leave three weeks saved.
He compares **paid hours**, rent and buses before taking another desk.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** picture could end most paid calls before another rent-covering job appears.
whatWouldHelp: Written **paid hours** and a posted local job covering rent after bus fare would help.
